newsitem.title: UK: Stocks battle bonds for funds' favours.
newsitem.headline: Stocks battle bonds for funds' favours.

text.p: Stock markets around the world have powered to new heights in recent weeks, raising the stakes in the battle between debt and equity investments.
Some analysts say now is the time to take at least some of the cash from share gains and plug it into debt markets, which they say will outpace equities over the medium term.
"If I had to jump, I'd say the economic environment for bonds is probably slightly better on a three- to six-month view," David Hewitt, bond strategist at Bank of Tokyo in London, said on Thursday.

Looking in particular at the United States, where the Dow Jones industrial average of leading shares has charted a steady rise since 1987 and is now hovering above 5,900 points after flirting with 6,000 earlier this week, Hewitt said there may be some danger ahead for equity investors.
"The U.S. economy is actually showing signs of slowing down, and with a rising dollar we might get some disappointing news on (corporate) earnings in the U.S.," he said.
If the the U.S. economy does slow, debt markets will enjoy the low interest rate and low inflation environment, but stock markets may be unsettled if corporate earnings are hit.

Analysts said that while both equities and debt were being buoyed by a global environment of subdued inflation, low borrowing costs and sustained growth, shares were looking overstretched -- perhaps pricing in too much positive news.
Like the Dow, Britain's FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX share indices have reached new record highs in the recent weeks.
Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International in London, agreed that bonds were more likely to give better returns in the next six months.

"The problem with equities -- particularly the higher priced equity markets -- is that if anything untoward happened to suggest the global low interest rate environment wouldn't persist, they will be vulnerable," he said.
"Equity markets are feeding off the low interest rate environment -- and if that is taken away from them, they are more vulnerable than bonds."
But analysts said the relative attractions of the two investment camps were a close call, and did not expect to see major shifts of funds from one to the other for the moment.
Hewitt said investment in U.S. equities, for example, was now based generally an a more long-term view than it used to be.

"It is not speculative money," he said. "So even though the valuations look a bit stretched, you're not necessarily going to see a big correction. The equity market is held in much firmer hands now than it was during the late 80s."

"I don't think we're really going to see much flow out of equities into bonds. The big U.S. brokers are revising up their forecasts for the Dow -- talking about another 10 percent from current levels -- so no-one is really expecting a big crash."
Paul Meader, director of Matheson Investment Management, was sceptical about the pulling power of world bond markets.
"What is driving bond markets at the moment is not really fundamentals, but simply a weight of money," he said.

Convergence plays between peripheral and core European debt, along with a market reassessment of previously bond-bearish predictions for U.S. interest rates, had recently coaxed investors who had been on the sidelines back to bonds, he said.

But Meader said the fundamental background for debt rallies was not solid enough to rely on. "If you look at the U.S. economy, I don't think we know any more about it now than we did a few weeks back. There is still a good chance U.S. rates will have to rise, and in that environment its going to be hard for bond markets to rally."
"Equity markets are a much more favourable place to have money in the longer-term than bond markets. Certainly our asset allocation is slanted very firmly towards equities."
